title: BCCI Bans U-19 Spinner for Age Fraud as Bengal Cricket Flags 62 Players
excerpt: The Cricket Association of Bengal has declared 62 players ineligible over age and documentation discrepancies, including a member of India's 2022 Under-19 World Cup-winning squad.
body:
• The BCCI has imposed a two-year ban on Bengal leg-spinner Rohit Yadav after finding he possessed three birth certificates with different years of birth — 2007, 2009, and 2010.
  • The Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB) has declared 62 players ineligible for registration or transfer during the 2026-27 and 2027-28 seasons over documentation and age discrepancies.
  • Former India Under-19 World Cup winner Ravi Kumar is among those flagged, with a 45-month age discrepancy in CAB records.
  • The crackdown is part of a wider effort to restore integrity to age-group cricket in India, where falsified records have been a persistent concern.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India has banned Bengal leg-spinner Rohit Yadav from domestic cricket for two years after investigations revealed multiple birth certificates with conflicting years of birth — a case that has exposed the scale of age fraud in Indian grassroots cricket.

Yadav, originally from Uttar Pradesh, had been selected for India's Under-19 squad for the upcoming series against Australia. He was part of the U-19 team that toured Sri Lanka in July, where he claimed six wickets and helped India win the final Test. The age discrepancy came to light when his documents were scrutinized during the Sri Lanka tour.

Three Birth Certificates, Multiple Aadhaar Entries

According to BCCI and Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB) records, Yadav has three birth certificates listing birth years of 2007, 2009, and 2010. His Aadhaar records compound the confusion: when he registered with the CAB, his birth year was recorded as 2007. Subsequent Aadhaar updates showed 2006 in 2017 and 2020 before changing to 2009 in 2021.

"He has been banned for two years."

— BCCI source

The CAB had previously flagged the discrepancies and kept Yadav out of its junior teams before informing the BCCI. The Board has now barred him from all domestic cricket and notified every affiliated state association. He has been removed from the India U-19 squad for the Australia series, with matches scheduled in Rajkot and Ahmedabad later this month.

62 Players Declared Ineligible

Yadav's case is part of a sweeping crackdown by the CAB, which has declared 62 players ineligible for registration or transfer for any tournament during the 2026-27 and 2027-28 domestic seasons. The list was compiled following a broader audit of player documentation and age records.

Among the most prominent names is Ravi Kumar, a left-arm fast bowler who played a decisive role in India's 2022 Under-19 World Cup triumph in the West Indies. Kumar took 4 for 34 in the final against England and finished the tournament with 10 wickets in six matches. CAB records show a 45-month age discrepancy in his documentation, affecting participation records spanning the 2021-22 through 2025-26 seasons across Under-19, Under-23, and senior categories.

Left-arm spin all-rounder Vishal Bhatti, who has three first-class and two List A appearances, is also on the list.

Discrepancies Stretching Years

The scale of the irregularities extends beyond a few high-profile cases. According to CAB's published list, some players have birth-date discrepancies spanning nearly a decade. One player, Arun Kumar Chawrasia, reportedly has a discrepancy of 115 months — more than 9.5 years. Another, Mahipal Yadav, shows a gap exceeding eight years.

The CAB said in a statement that it "remains committed to ensuring proper verification and adherence to the prescribed regulations governing age-group cricket" and has pledged to follow rigorous verification protocols going forward.

A Persistent Problem

Age fraud has been a longstanding issue in Indian cricket, where over-age players competing in youth tournaments can distort competition and block genuinely eligible players. The practice is enabled by inconsistencies in India's identity documentation system, where multiple birth certificates and conflicting government records are not uncommon.

The BCCI's willingness to ban a player who had already represented India at the Under-19 level — and the CAB's decision to flag a World Cup winner — suggests cricket authorities are taking a harder line than in the past. Whether the crackdown extends beyond Bengal remains to be seen.
